plot_extraction.response_text:
At a remote British station in India, the arrogant but eligible Saumarez courts two closely attached sisters, Maud and Edith Copleigh. Everyone assumes he intends to marry Maud, the elder and more conventionally charming sister, though both women appear drawn to him.

During a moonlight riding picnic, a violent dust storm plunges the party into darkness. Believing he is speaking to Edith, whom he has secretly loved all along, Saumarez proposes—only to discover that he has proposed to Maud. Overjoyed, Maud accepts, while Edith, having overheard the proposal, flees on horseback in despair.

Saumarez confesses his mistake to the narrator, who prevents him from immediately abandoning Maud and rides after Edith. After a dangerous chase through the storm, Edith’s horse goes lame. The narrator explains that Saumarez truly loves her and persuades her to return.

At dawn, they reach the picnic site, where Saumarez publicly kisses Edith, making his real choice clear. The assembled guests applaud, and the party rides home in newly arranged couples, leaving Maud’s humiliation and her version of events untold.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story uses a clubbable, anecdotal first-person style in which an observant male insider recounts a colonial social mishap while repeatedly admitting that his knowledge is partial. The narrator speaks for a collective “we” as often as for himself, presenting the isolated Anglo-Indian Station as a small, gossip-driven community with its own assumptions, rituals, and slang. His tone combines worldly confidence with self-mockery: he offers maxims about courtship and women, then undercuts his authority by insisting that men are blind in such matters and that the “woman’s version” remains inaccessible. Direct addresses such as “Would you believe it” and “You must not laugh at this” make the tale resemble an after-dinner story told to a familiar audience.

The narrative voice is ironic, aphoristic, and socially satirical. Characters are introduced through brisk verdicts rather than extended psychological analysis: Saumarez is vain, efficient, and “summary” by nature; the sisters are assessed according to the Station’s marriage-market judgments. Bureaucratic language is humorously transferred to romance when Saumarez “drafted his Resolution” and formed a “Select Committee of One.” Similar incongruities animate the comparisons with ponies, polo, official councils, and military staff. The narrator’s generalisations about gender are deliberately sweeping and period-bound, reflecting the masculine conventions and prejudices of the colonial milieu while also exposing their limitations.

The diction shifts effectively between conversational plainness and heightened descriptive prose. Social passages rely on colloquial expressions, parenthetical qualifications, dry understatement, and local or institutional terms such as “Civilian,” “Station,” “Hills,” “pagri,” and “rupees.” In the storm sequence, the language becomes sensory, kinetic, and near-apocalyptic. Verbs such as “lashing,” “roaring,” “whirling,” “thrashing,” and “spurting” give the weather violent agency, while images of the Day of Judgment, the Pit, lost souls, and the end of the world enlarge a romantic misunderstanding into a moment of cosmic disorder. Heat, dust, lightning, sweat, darkness, and noise are rendered with physical intensity.

Sentence structure follows this tonal movement. The social exposition often uses balanced, elaborately qualified sentences whose clauses reproduce the narrator’s habit of revising or contradicting himself. Aphorisms and short judgments punctuate these longer constructions. During the storm and pursuit, coordination and accumulation accelerate the rhythm: repeated “and” clauses convey confusion, breathlessness, and sensory overload. Capitalisation in dialogue—“I WANT to go home,” “HER,” and “WOULD”—records shouted emphasis and emotional extremity, while dashes, semicolons, italics, and exclamation marks preserve the energy of oral narration.

The plot is tightly constructed around concealment, mistaken identity, and reversal. The opening establishes that Saumarez is expected to propose to the elder sister; the sisters’ physical and vocal resemblance makes the error plausible; the moonlight picnic supplies a socially sanctioned courtship setting; and the dust-storm removes sight, privacy, and ordinary restraint at exactly the crucial moment. The narrative then changes from comedy of manners to elemental melodrama and finally returns to social comedy. This progression is mirrored by the weather: oppressive heat corresponds to emotional tension, the storm precipitates confession and confusion, and the cleared dawn restores conventional identities and behaviour.

Dialogue is sparse but dramatically concentrated. Most of the story is mediated through the narrator’s commentary, so the sudden cries and shouted exchanges in the darkness have exceptional force. Edith’s repeated wish to go home initially appears to be fear of the storm, then acquires its true emotional meaning. Saumarez’s blunt confession—“I’ve proposed to the wrong one!”—compresses the central reversal into a comic line. The narrator’s failure to produce an adequate response reinforces the sense that the storm has temporarily suspended reason and etiquette.

Characterisation is largely external and social. People are defined by reputation, appearance, income, manner, and conduct rather than by sustained interior monologue. Edith’s hidden vulnerability is revealed through action and breakdown; Maud’s happiness is captured in a sudden lyrical image; and Saumarez’s emotional confusion appears physically in his shaking, clawing grip, and drawn face. The narrator himself becomes an accidental “Providence,” meddling out of a confused desire to make events proceed “decently and in order.” His retrospective embarrassment prevents him from assuming the status of an uncomplicated hero.

The dominant effects are comic irony, atmospheric suspense, and emotional release. The proposal to the wrong sister is farcical, but Edith’s flight gives the mistake genuine pain and urgency. The theatrical reunion, complete with ghostlike spectators applauding beneath the trees, is both moving and faintly absurd. Repeated claims that the experience was dreamlike, unnatural, or “out of the world” frame the night as a temporary suspension of English reserve. By dawn, the participants return to ordinary social roles, and the heightened episode recedes into communal legend.

The story’s frame is self-conscious and metafictional. It begins by declaring that the exact truth cannot be known because the decisive female perspective is unavailable to the male narrator, and it ends by returning to that absence. This circular structure casts doubt on everything between: the account is vivid and authoritative in manner, yet explicitly “from the outside” and therefore potentially “all wrong.” The verse epigraph establishes an elevated mood of earthly expectation and shared disturbance, which the prose then translates into the smaller but emotionally charged world of courtship. Overall, the style blends oral anecdote, colonial comedy of manners, masculine self-satire, romantic melodrama, and powerful meteorological description.

### THE ERROR OF MR. SAUMAREZ

*When the hot earth waits for thunder,*  
*And the heart for leave to speak,*  
*Who shall say what god or blunder*  
*Turns the strong aside to seek?*

There are three accounts of the Saumarez affair, and they are all untrue. The Station held one, Saumarez supplied another in fragments and under pressure, and I have constructed the third from what I saw, heard, guessed, and was afterwards requested to forget. The women’s account would settle the matter; but women do not render departmental reports upon their hearts, and, if they did, no man would understand the handwriting.

Therefore you must take this as an outside narrative.

Saumarez was the best match within three hundred miles—excluding a Lieutenant-Governor who had a wife in England and a liver in Calcutta. He was young for his appointment, drew a respectable number of rupees monthly, played polo without apology, and possessed that clean, finished manner which convinces elderly ladies that a man has principles. He had also a straight nose, a light hand with a horse, and rather too complete a knowledge of both advantages.

We forgave him because the Station was small.

In the rains, when the roads went out in sections and the dak arrived smelling of mildew, we discussed one another. In the cold weather, when strangers came through, we discussed them. In the hot weather, when no decent brain should be required to operate after ten in the morning, we discussed everybody from the Chief Commissioner to the last joined subaltern. A Station is a Select Committee perpetually in session, without minutes, chairman, or power of adjournment.

The Copleigh girls arrived in November to keep house for their father, old Copleigh of the Canal Department, whose ideas on irrigation had been rejected by three Governments and adopted, without acknowledgment, by a fourth. Maud was twenty-four, Edith twenty-one, and they were devoted to each other in that alarming fashion which makes an outsider feel he has interrupted a private service.

Maud was the prettier by all accepted measurements. She had warm brown hair, a colour that survived luncheon, a laugh audible across a tennis-ground, and the invaluable gift of appearing pleased with the person before her. Edith was slighter and quieter. At first one remembered only her grey eyes and the trick she had of looking down before answering; afterwards one remembered exactly what she had said. Their voices were alike enough to deceive anyone who could not see their faces, and, when they rode in broad hats and pale habits, a man meeting them against the sun had to wait for the laugh. If it rang out promptly, the rider was Maud. If there came a pause and then some little edged remark, it was Edith.

That distinction, plain to us in daylight, cost four people a night’s peace and very nearly one life.

Saumarez began to call at the Copleighs’. There was nothing remarkable in that. Every unmarried man called there, and several married ones went with messages from their wives which required an hour to deliver. But Saumarez called systematically. He lent Maud books, reserved dances for Maud, chose Maud’s side at tennis, and once rode nine miles to bring Maud a spray of hill jasmine which had ceased to be jasmine before it arrived.

The Station drafted its Resolution.

Saumarez would marry Maud.

You must not laugh at us. Society in exile lives by conclusions, as a man in the desert lives by water, and is not particular about purity. Mrs. Deane said the matter had been arranged at Simla. The Padre’s wife said she had observed a Spiritual Understanding. Young Prendergast of the Police offered two to one on an engagement before the rains. Even old Copleigh began enlarging a bungalow in his mind and complaining that married officers expected too many shelves.

Only Edith appeared untouched. She was always with Maud, of course, and often with Saumarez; but she moved at the edge of their talk, smiling when appealed to, silent when forgotten. Now and again I caught Saumarez watching her. Since men are idiots where two sisters are concerned, I supposed he was wondering whether she approved of him.

In justice to men, women sometimes take pains to keep us idiots.

The heat came early that year. By April the sky had hardened to brass, the plains trembled from noon till evening, and the crows sat with their beaks open in the tamarinds, too exhausted to abuse the world. We ate, slept, and quarrelled beneath punkahs. The horses went out before sunrise and after moonrise, and anyone who suggested exertion between those hours was regarded as a criminal lunatic.

It was Mrs. Deane who arranged the riding picnic. She had a genius for entertainment and catastrophe, and rarely produced one without the other.

We were to start at nine in the evening, ride to the old tombs beyond the dry river, dine beneath the peepul trees, and return by moonlight. There were fourteen of us, with servants, hampers, lanterns, rugs, and enough soda-water to float a district officer. The moon was nearly full. A wind had been restless all day, but no one minded that. In the hot weather one welcomes any movement in the air, even if it comes to remove the roof.

Saumarez rode beside Maud as we left the Station, and Edith kept with me for the first two miles. She talked too quickly and laughed twice where there was no occasion.

“You are over-tired,” I said, with the heavy tact of an old friend.

“I am perfectly well.”

“That is what people say before fainting.”

“Then I shall try to be original.”

After that she rode ahead and joined her sister. The three moved together in the white dust, their shadows running black and enormous across the road. I remember thinking that Saumarez had the air of a man escorted to his own wedding by two possible brides.

At the tombs we spread dinner in the ruins of a garden built by some forgotten prince who had understood shade better than the Public Works Department. The dome of the chief tomb shone like bone in the moonlight. Bats clicked within it; jackals called from the river-bed; and the servants moved among the trees with lanterns that made their white clothes flare and vanish.

We were all more cheerful than was reasonable. Heat and moonlight loosen English tongues abroad. Mrs. Deane sang half a song; the Padre told a story unsuitable to his coat; and young Prendergast attempted to open champagne with a cavalry sabre. Through it all Saumarez was grave and absent, and I saw him once stand alone by the ruined wall, looking towards the sisters.

He had, as I learned later, drafted his Resolution. He had considered the matter for six weeks, balanced objections, reviewed precedents, and formed a Select Committee of One. This is how an efficient man goes mad.

At eleven the wind dropped.

The leaves turned their pale undersides and hung still. Far away, beyond the river, a brown bar lay across the stars.

One of the servants touched my elbow. “Andhi, sahib.”

I saw the cooks tying cloths over the baskets and the syces catching at the bridles.

Mrs. Deane said, “A dust-storm? How delicious!”

That is the kind of thing people say before Nature answers them personally.

The brown bar rose. It climbed without sound at first, blotting out the low stars and then the high ones, until half the world was gone. The moon burned red above it. The horses lifted their heads, snuffing, and one began to back among the plates.

Then the wind struck.

It came across the river-bed like the advance of artillery—roaring, lashing, and carrying half the plain before it. The trees bent with a single crack of leaves. Lanterns went out. Rugs, napkins, hats, and paper plates sprang into the air and were whirled towards the tombs. Someone shouted to hold the horses; someone else screamed that the hampers were rolling downhill; and Prendergast, who had found no better use for his sabre, cut a guy-rope and brought the dinner-cloth over the Padre’s head.

In ten seconds there was no moon, no road, no party, and, so far as the senses could testify, no British Empire.

Dust filled the mouth and eyes. It drove like hot shot against the face and crept beneath collar, cuff, and pagri. The peepul branches thrashed above us; the horses plunged and snorted; women called names that the wind tore apart; and the blackness moved—solid, choking, alive. Lightning flickered somewhere behind the dust, not in strokes but in vast red pulses, as though the Pit had opened and shut its furnace doors.

I caught a bridle, lost it, collided with a tree, and embraced, successively, a frightened bearer and the Padre. Neither thanked me. Then a woman’s voice cried close at hand—

“I WANT to go home!”

It was Edith, as I believed, though in that uproar one might have mistaken Gabriel for a railway guard.

“Stay where you are!” I shouted.

“I WANT to go home!”

A man answered her. I heard Saumarez’s voice, sharp and commanding, and saw for an instant, by the red flare of lightning, two figures pressed into the lee of the tomb wall. Then the dust shut them away.

I turned towards the horses, where confusion had become mutiny. A syce was hanging to Maud’s mare; Prendergast’s Waler had broken loose; Mrs. Deane sat calmly on a hamper with her skirt over her head; and old Copleigh, who had not attended the picnic, was being loudly blamed for all of it.

There came a lull—not quiet, but a drawing of breath before the next assault. Through it I heard Saumarez say, very distinctly—

“I have tried not to tell you. I cannot. I love you. Will you marry me?”

A woman sobbed once and answered, “Yes.”

There are moments when one knows that the Station has been justified and feels no pleasure in it. I looked away. The wind returned, the trees bowed, and the whole night went mad again.

Five minutes later—perhaps fifteen; clocks have no authority in a dust-storm—someone clutched my arm. Saumarez’s face showed pale in a flicker of lightning. His eyes were full of dust and horror.

“Come here,” he said.

“I am here.”

“Not here—away from them.”

He dragged me behind a broken screen of masonry and gripped both my shoulders. He was shaking. Saumarez, who had played the last chukker of a cup-tie with a cracked collar-bone, shook like a novice before inspection.

“I’ve proposed to the wrong one!”

“What?”

“The wrong one! I thought it was Edith. It was Maud.”

For once in my life I had no maxim ready. I opened my mouth, and the dust filled it.

“She said yes,” he went on. “She put her arms round me. Then the lightning came, and I saw—HER.”

“You proposed to Maud?”

“I have told you!”

“But everyone expected—”

“Everyone is a fool. I love Edith. I have always loved Edith.”

This was unfair, because he had taken great pains to instruct everyone otherwise; but a man in extremity blames the nearest public.

“Where is Maud now?”

“With Mrs. Deane. Happy—Good God, you should have seen her face! I must tell her at once.”

“You will do nothing of the kind.”

“I will tell her it was a mistake.”

“You will tell a woman, five minutes after she has accepted you, that you mistook her for her sister?”

“Yes.”

“Then I shall hit you with a stone.”

Do not suppose I reasoned nobly. I had no more plan than a goat in a flooded nullah. I only knew that certain things are not done, and that if they must be done they should not be done in public, in a storm, beside the remains of a trifle and fourteen witnesses.

Saumarez clawed at my sleeve. “Edith heard.”

“How do you know?”

“She was near us. I saw her when the lightning came.”

At that instant a horse broke from the group with a squeal and a hammering of hoofs. A rider bent low over its neck. The next red pulse showed Edith’s pale habit flying against the darkness.

“Miss Edith!” a syce cried.

She was gone towards the river road.

Saumarez made for his horse. I held him.

“Let me go!”

“And leave Maud here while you gallop after her sister? The Station would have to invent a new Commandment.”

“She’ll kill herself.”

“Stay with Maud.”

I do not know why he obeyed. Perhaps my hand was on his bridle; perhaps, beneath all his selfishness, he saw what his going would proclaim. I mounted the first horse that could be persuaded to face the wind. It happened to be Prendergast’s Waler, a long, hard-mouthed brute that disliked me and civilisation equally.

“I’ll bring her back,” I said.

This was pure boasting. I could not see the road.

We went down into the storm.

The Waler fought for his head, and I let him have enough to choose the ground. Dust whirled in columns, broke, and whirled again. The dry branches came flying out of nowhere. Once a sheet of thorn-scrub rolled across our path like some many-legged beast, and the horse rose beneath me. Lightning pulsed behind the murk, turning every grain of dust blood-red, then dead black. There was no horizon. Earth and sky had been ground together, and we rode through the mill.

I listened for hoofs. The roaring swallowed everything; then, in a lull, I caught the faint hard beat ahead.

“Edith!”

No answer.

We crossed the dry channel at a slant, sliding among loose stones. On the farther bank the Waler stumbled to his knees, recovered, and bolted. I had branches across my face, reins burning through my fingers, and the firm conviction that the Day of Judgment had come by circular order and omitted to state the place of assembly.

Again I heard hoofs—nearer now, irregular.

“EDITH!”

A cry came back, thin as a lost soul’s.

“I WANT to go home!”

She did not mean the Copleigh bungalow. I knew that much, though I knew nothing else.

Her mare showed suddenly in front of us, swerved, and almost fell. I dragged the Waler across her path. Edith struck at him with her whip.

“Let me pass!”

“Your mare is lame.”

“I don’t care.”

“She does.”

“I WANT to go home!”

“Yes, yes. All Englishwomen want to go home in April. Get down.”

She tried to wheel away. The mare took three steps and stood trembling, her near foreleg held clear of the ground. Edith slipped from the saddle—or fell; I cannot say—and faced me with both hands clenched. Dust had plastered her hair across her cheeks. She looked very young and very terrible.

“You heard?” I shouted.

“I heard enough.”

“He thought you were Maud.”

She laughed. There was no amusement in it.

“Of course.”

“He meant to ask you.”

“Of course.”

“He loves you.”

“OF COURSE!”

Each answer cut like a whip. Then she turned away and leaned her forehead against the mare’s saddle.

I continued, because Providence, when compelled to use a middle-aged bachelor, must accept clumsy instruments.

“He has loved you all along. He behaved like a fool to hide it.”

“He made Maud love him.”

“I don’t know.”

“I do.”

This is the point at which the woman’s story begins, and I cannot give it. What passed between the sisters in looks, silences, denials, and those midnight councils from which men are excluded may have altered every fact I carried. Perhaps Maud knew. Perhaps Edith had sacrificed herself. Perhaps each believed she was shielding the other. A man sees two women kiss and thinks the matter simple.

“He has asked her,” Edith said. “She accepted him. That ends it.”

“Nothing ended tonight. Nothing could. The world itself has gone out of order.”

“He must marry her.”

“Would you marry a man who loved Maud?”

She lifted her head at that.

It was a brutal question, but brutality sometimes enters where tact sits knocking. The wind slackened. The dust still streamed past us, but overhead a ragged space opened, and one star looked down with the indecency of a spectator.

“He cannot humiliate her,” Edith said.

“He has done that already, though she does not know it. If he marries her, he will repeat the humiliation every day.”

She covered her face. I heard no sobbing; only the small, exhausted breath of someone who has held herself rigid too long.

“He called me Edith,” she whispered.

“When?”

“After she said yes. The wind took it. Maud did not hear.”

There it was—the entire case, appeal, and judgment in one sentence.

We stood among the flying dust while the mare trembled and the Waler tried to bite her. Then Edith said, “Take me back.”

We led the lame mare and rode by turns. The storm travelled eastward, grumbling like a defeated army. Behind it the moon returned, blurred and yellow; then the stars came out by companies. The plain had changed colour. Broken branches lay across the track, and the dust covered everything in one ghostly livery—horse, rider, thorn, and stone.

Near dawn the air grew almost cold. Edith rode before me on the Waler, straight-backed and silent. I walked beside the mare and wondered what I had done. There are men born to administer districts, men born to command regiments, and men born to interfere in love-affairs. The last should be drowned early.

At the tombs the party had reassembled beneath the trees. They looked like survivors of a siege—faces grey, clothes torn, hair full of leaves, dignity abandoned. Mrs. Deane had recovered her hat and lost one shoe. The Padre held a lantern though daylight was gathering. Maud sat on the low wall wrapped in Saumarez’s coat.

She was beautiful.

I say it because it is true, and because no one has ever properly remembered her in this affair. Happiness had cleared and softened her face. She watched the road with shining eyes, believing, as she had every right to believe, that her future had been settled.

Then she saw Edith.

Saumarez moved before anyone spoke. His face was drawn and dirty, and he walked like a man going to execution. Maud rose. Edith slipped from the saddle.

For one second the three stood together.

What Maud saw in her sister’s face, or in his, I cannot tell. Her own expression altered—only a little, only once. She put out a hand as though to steady herself against the wall.

Saumarez went past her.

He took Edith by both shoulders and kissed her before us all.

It was an outrageous act—un-English, unregulated, and wholly conclusive.

Someone began to clap. I believe it was Mrs. Deane. Prendergast followed, then the Padre, and in a moment the ghostly company beneath the peepuls were applauding as though the curtain had fallen upon a comedy. Perhaps relief made us cruel. Perhaps we wished to force a happy ending upon what we did not understand. At dawn, after a storm, mankind will applaud almost anything that proves the world continues.

Edith hid her face against Saumarez’s coat.

Maud stood very still.

Then Mrs. Deane crossed to her, put an arm about her waist, and spoke too low for me to hear. Maud smiled. It was a perfect Station smile—brave, easy, and fit to be discussed over breakfast. If you ask me what it cost, I cannot tell you.

We rode home in newly arranged couples. Saumarez went with Edith. Mrs. Deane kept Maud beside her. The Padre took charge of the lame mare. I returned Prendergast’s Waler, who had bitten me twice and saved one life, and was thanked as though I had borrowed a newspaper.

By eight o’clock the Station knew there had been an engagement. By luncheon it knew there had been a misunderstanding. By evening it had decided that Saumarez and Edith had always been intended for each other and that Maud had never seriously cared for him. This last conclusion was necessary to our comfort, and therefore became official.

Saumarez married Edith in the cold weather. They were happy, I think; but happiness within marriage is another department, and I have never held that appointment.

As for Maud, she went to the Hills, and later there were reports of a Major in the Guides, a man with a scar and private means. Perhaps she married him. Perhaps she did not. The Station preferred that she should, because society dislikes an unpaid account.

I have told you what Saumarez confessed, what Edith cried in the storm, and what we applauded beneath the trees. But I do not know what Maud said to Edith afterwards, nor why she smiled at dawn, nor whether the wrong proposal was altogether a mistake in her eyes.

That is the missing account—the woman’s version.

Without it, this story may be true.

It may also be all wrong.

### The Museum of Unfinished Things

On the first Tuesday of every month, the Museum of Unfinished Things opened its doors precisely at midnight.

It stood at the end of Bellweather Street, between a bakery that had been closed for thirty years and a narrow house with no windows. During daylight, the museum looked abandoned. Dust clouded its tall glass doors, weeds pushed through the steps, and a brass sign above the entrance displayed only three words:

**NOT YET COMPLETE**

Most people passed without noticing it. Those who did notice soon forgot.

But at midnight on the first Tuesday, lamps glowed behind the dusty windows. The weeds drew back from the steps. The brass letters shone. And Mr. Vale, the museum’s only curator, unlocked the doors.

He was a thin man with silver hair, a black suit, and a pocket watch that had no hands. He never advertised the museum, yet visitors always came.

Some arrived carrying half-written letters. Some brought broken machines they had once intended to repair. Others carried songs without endings, plans for gardens never planted, wedding dresses never worn, or apologies they had rehearsed but never spoken.

Mr. Vale accepted almost everything.

He placed each item in a glass case, wrote a small card, and displayed it in one of the museum’s endless halls.

There was a model ship whose maker had died before adding the sails. There was a symphony missing its final note. There was a staircase built by a carpenter who had never decided where it should lead. There were portraits with blank faces, clocks without numbers, and a chess game abandoned one move before checkmate.

Visitors often asked Mr. Vale why he collected unfinished things.

“Because completed things belong to the world,” he would say. “Unfinished things belong to possibility.”

Then, one rainy Tuesday night, a girl named Mara arrived carrying a jar.

She was thirteen years old, wore a yellow coat two sizes too large, and had walked three miles through the storm. Water streamed from her dark hair. Mud covered her boots.

Mr. Vale opened the door before she could knock.

“You’re late,” he said.

Mara looked past him into the glowing entrance hall. “The sign says you open at midnight.”

“It is twelve-oh-seven.”

“My bicycle chain broke.”

“Then your bicycle is unfinished?”

“No. It’s broken.”

“Ah.” Mr. Vale stepped aside. “That is a different museum.”

Mara entered.

The jar in her arms was sealed with red wax. It was an ordinary preserving jar, the sort used for peaches or jam, but something faintly luminous moved inside it.

Mr. Vale noticed at once.

“What have you brought me?”

“A summer,” Mara said.

He raised one silver eyebrow.

“My brother’s last summer.”

The rain tapped softly against the windows. Somewhere deep in the museum, a bell rang once.

Mr. Vale extended both hands. “May I?”

Mara hesitated, then passed him the jar.

It was warm. Inside, pale gold light swirled like mist. When Mr. Vale held it near his ear, he heard distant waves, gulls, and two children laughing.

He looked at Mara carefully. “Where did you get this?”

“I caught it.”

“That is not usually possible.”

“I used my mother’s preserving recipe.”

“For summer?”

“For apricots. I changed it.”

Mr. Vale turned the jar. Tiny shapes flickered behind the glass: a red kite, a wooden pier, a blue bucket, a boy running barefoot along a beach.

The label, written in a child’s uneven handwriting, read:

**JULY—BEFORE EVERYTHING CHANGED**

“What was left unfinished?” Mr. Vale asked.

Mara stared at the floor.

“My brother, Eli, wanted to swim to the black rock. It was far from shore, and our mother said he was too young. He promised we would do it together before the summer ended.”

“But you did not.”

“He got sick.”

Mr. Vale waited.

“He died in September.”

The golden light in the jar dimmed.

Mara quickly took it back and held it against her chest.

“I don’t want you to keep it forever,” she said. “I only want you to put it somewhere safe.”

“Safe from what?”

“From me.”

Mr. Vale’s expression changed, though only slightly.

“Explain.”

“Sometimes I open it.”

“You open the jar?”

“Only a little. Just enough to smell the sea.”

“That is unwise.”

“I know.”

“No,” said Mr. Vale. “I do not think you do.”

He turned and walked toward the nearest gallery. With no better choice, Mara followed.

They passed a collection of unwritten novels, their blank pages fluttering behind glass. They crossed a room filled with inventions that almost worked. A pair of mechanical wings beat slowly near the ceiling, lifting no one. In another hall, hundreds of locked doors stood without walls.

At last, Mr. Vale stopped before an empty case.

“Unfinished memories are dangerous,” he said. “They do not remain unchanged. Each time you visit them, they borrow something from the present.”

Mara frowned. “Memories can’t do that.”

“Most cannot. Yours has been preserved.”

“I only go back for a minute.”

“And when you return?”

She did not answer.

Mr. Vale leaned closer. “What have you forgotten?”

“Nothing.”

“Your teacher’s name?”

Mara opened her mouth.

No answer came.

“The color of your bedroom?”

She looked down, frightened.

“Your mother’s voice?”

“I know her voice.”

“Then describe it.”

Mara gripped the jar until her fingers whitened.

In her mind, her mother’s voice should have been easy to find. It had called her downstairs for breakfast that morning. It had reminded her to take an umbrella. Yet when Mara searched for its sound, she found only the cry of gulls and Eli shouting from the beach.

“That’s why I brought it,” she whispered.

Mr. Vale unlocked the glass case.

“You may leave it here.”

“For how long?”

“As long as you need.”

“Will I be able to visit?”

“On the first Tuesday.”

“Can I open it?”

“No.”

Mara stepped toward the case, but before she could place the jar inside, something knocked from within it.

Once.

Twice.

Then a boy’s voice, faint but clear, called, “Mara?”

She froze.

Mr. Vale’s face became grave. “Do not answer.”

“Mara!” the voice called again. “Come on! The water’s warm!”

Her eyes filled with tears.

“That’s Eli.”

“It is an echo.”

“He sounds real.”

“Echoes often do.”

Inside the jar, the summer brightened. A tiny shoreline unfolded beneath the glass. Eli stood ankle-deep in glittering water, waving.

Beyond him, black against the sunset, rose a lonely rock.

Mara put her thumb against the wax seal.

Mr. Vale caught her wrist.

“If you open it now, the memory will take more than a teacher’s name.”

“I have to go.”

“You have already gone many times.”

“We never reached the rock.”

“And you never will.”

Anger flashed across Mara’s face. “You collect unfinished things. Why won’t you let me finish this?”

“Because finishing the past destroys the present.”

“You don’t know that.”

“I know it better than anyone.”

For the first time, Mr. Vale looked old. Not elderly, but ancient—as though the years had been waiting behind his eyes and had suddenly stepped forward.

He released her wrist.

“Come,” he said.

He led Mara beyond the public galleries, through a narrow door marked **CURATOR ONLY**.

Behind it lay a staircase descending into darkness.

They went down for a long time. The air grew cold. The sounds of the museum faded until Mara could hear only their footsteps and the soft murmur of the sea inside her jar.

At the bottom stood a circular room.

Unlike the galleries above, it contained a single object: a small white door in a silver frame.

There was no wall around it.

The door was slightly open, and warm daylight shone through the gap.

Mr. Vale stopped several feet away.

“This is mine,” he said.

“Your unfinished thing?”

“Yes.”

“What’s behind it?”

“My home.”

Mara looked at him. “You live in the museum.”

“Now I do.”

He drew the handless watch from his pocket.

“Long ago, I was a clockmaker. I had a wife named Adeline and a little boy named Simon. One winter morning, I left home after an argument. It was a foolish argument. I cannot remember what it was about, only that I wanted to win it.”

He rubbed the watch’s smooth face.

“I went to my workshop. That afternoon, a fire swept through our street.”

Mara looked toward the white door.

“This is the last moment before I left,” Mr. Vale said. “Adeline is in the kitchen. Simon is building a castle beneath the table. If I step through, I can stay. I can apologize. I can warn them.”

“Why don’t you?”

“I tried.”

The daylight beyond the door flickered.

“I returned to that morning hundreds of times. In one version, I stopped the fire. In another, I sent my family away. In another, I caught the man who knocked over the lamp that started it. Each time I changed the memory, it consumed part of my life.”

“What parts?”

“My childhood. My friends. The first clock I ever made. My mother’s face. Eventually, I forgot the sound of Adeline’s laughter—the very thing I had been trying to save.”

He closed his fingers around the watch.

“The past does not permit repairs. It accepts only exchanges.”

Mara looked at the jar. Eli still waited in the golden water, calling her name.

“If you knew it was dangerous, why did you keep the door?”

“Because knowing is not the same as letting go.”

A gust of salty air swept through the underground room.

The red wax on Mara’s jar cracked.

Mr. Vale spun around.

A thin line of gold appeared beneath the lid.

Eli’s voice filled the chamber.

“Mara! Hurry!”

The jar had been opened too many times. The memory no longer needed her permission.

The lid burst free.

Summer poured out.

Sunlight struck the stone floor. Sand spread beneath Mara’s boots. The circular room vanished under a bright blue sky, and suddenly she was standing on the beach exactly as it had been three years before.

Mr. Vale was gone.

So was the museum.

Mara looked down. Her boots had become bare feet. Her yellow coat had disappeared. She wore her old green swimsuit, the one with the crooked strap her mother had promised to mend.

Eli stood beside her.

He was ten again, brown-haired and sunburned, grinning as he held out his hand.

“You took forever,” he said.

Mara could not breathe.

She touched his face.

Warm.

Real.

He laughed and pulled away. “What are you doing?”

She threw her arms around him.

Eli made an embarrassed sound. “Mara, stop.”

But after a moment, he hugged her back.

She remembered this day. Their mother was reading beneath a striped umbrella. A radio played near the lifeguard station. The air smelled of coconut lotion and hot sand.

Far out in the water, the black rock waited.

“Ready?” Eli asked.

Mara looked toward the umbrella.

Their mother raised a hand and called something. The wind carried her words away.

Mara tried to remember her voice, but the memory had already begun to take it.

“Eli,” she said, “we shouldn’t.”

“You promised.”

“I know.”

“We can make it.”

Mara looked at him—at the water shining on his shoulders, at the tiny scar above his eyebrow, at his impatient smile.

She had wanted this every day since he died. One more hour. One more conversation. A chance to keep the promise.

Eli ran into the sea.

Mara followed.

The water rose around their knees, their waists, their shoulders. Then they began to swim.

At first, it was easy. The sea held them gently. Eli raced ahead, laughing whenever Mara splashed him.

But the black rock did not seem to come closer.

After several minutes, Mara looked back.

The beach was fading.

The striped umbrella had lost its colors. The lifeguard station blurred. Their mother stood at the edge of the water, but her face was blank.

Mara stopped swimming.

Every stroke toward the rock carried her deeper into the memory. Every second erased something waiting for her outside it.

She tried to think of home.

She could not remember the color of the front door.

She tried to picture her best friend.

A name appeared—Nina—then dissolved like foam.

Ahead, Eli reached the black rock and climbed onto it.

“We did it!” he shouted.

Mara floated between him and the disappearing shore.

“Come on!” he called.

Her arms felt heavy. Beneath the clear water, she saw things sinking into darkness: her schoolbooks, her bicycle, her mother’s favorite cup, a birthday cake with fourteen candles waiting to be lit next spring.

Her future.

“Mara!”

She swam toward the rock.

One stroke.

Two.

Eli leaned down, reaching for her.

If she took his hand, she knew she could stay. They could sit on the sun-warmed stone forever. The afternoon would never end. September would never come.

“Mara,” he said softly.

She reached up.

Their fingers almost touched.

Then she saw his expression.

It was not the impatient grin of the preserved memory. It was sad and knowing.

“You’re not Eli,” she said.

The boy tilted his head.

“You’re what I remember.”

“I’m enough,” he replied.

For one terrible moment, she wanted that to be true.

Then, from across the water, she heard a voice.

Not clear. Not yet familiar. But desperate.

Her mother was calling her home.

Mara turned away from the rock.

The boy grabbed her wrist.

“You promised!”

She pulled free.

“I know,” she sobbed. “But I can’t keep it.”

The sea darkened.

“You’ll lose me.”

“I already lost you.”

The words broke something.

The perfect summer cracked from horizon to horizon.

Mara swam.

Behind her, Eli called again, but his voice became the cry of a gull. Waves rose around her. The shore seemed impossibly distant.

As she fought toward it, she gathered fragments of her present from the water.

Her bicycle had a silver bell.

Her bedroom walls were green.

Her teacher was Mrs. Alden.

Nina laughed with a snort and hated oranges.

Her mother sang while washing dishes, always too quietly to hear the words.

Each recovered detail made the beach more solid.

At last, Mara’s feet struck sand.

Her mother stood before her, still faceless, arms outstretched.

Mara ran toward her.

The summer shattered.

She fell onto the cold floor of the museum’s underground room.

Glass rained around her, dissolving before it landed.

Mr. Vale knelt nearby, one hand braced against the silver frame of his white door. It had blown wide open.

Beyond it, a woman stood in a bright kitchen. A little boy crouched under the table, placing wooden blocks on top of one another.

“Papa!” the boy cried when he saw Mr. Vale.

The curator stared.

Mara understood. When her jar had broken, it had opened his memory too.

The woman turned. “Are you leaving without saying goodbye?”

Mr. Vale rose unsteadily.

His hand found the handless watch.

He looked at Mara. Then he looked at his family.

The longing on his face was so deep that Mara had to turn away.

“Papa?” Simon called.

Mr. Vale stepped toward the door.

He reached for the handle.

Then he gently pulled it closed.

The daylight narrowed to a golden thread and disappeared.

In the silence, the handless pocket watch began to tick.

Mr. Vale looked down in surprise.

Two black hands had appeared on its face.

The time was twelve forty-three.

For the first time in many years, it moved forward.

Mara sat up.

“My jar,” she said.

“Gone.”

“Is the summer gone too?”

“No.” Mr. Vale touched his chest. “Only unsealed.”

She searched her memory.

She could still see Eli standing on the black rock, but the image was softer now. Imperfect. He was missing a front tooth, though she had forgotten that before. His hair stuck up at the back. He was not glowing. He was not an echo calling her to stay.

He was simply her brother.

Mara began to cry.

Mr. Vale sat beside her and waited.

After a while, he offered her a clean white handkerchief.

“Will I forget him?” she asked.

“Some details.”

“I don’t want to.”

“You will remember others.”

“What if I forget his voice?”

“You may.”

“That’s horrible.”

“Yes.”

She looked at him sharply, expecting comfort.

Mr. Vale gave none.

Then he added, “But forgetting the exact sound of a voice is not the same as forgetting what it said.”

Mara wiped her eyes.

Above them, bells began to ring throughout the museum.

One after another, glass cases opened.

The unfinished symphony played its final note.

The mechanical wings folded and became still.

Behind the doors without walls, locks clicked. Half-written letters filled with ink, though whether they became apologies, confessions, or farewells, no one could say.

“What’s happening?” Mara asked.

Mr. Vale listened.

“The museum is closing.”

“Until next month?”

“No. I think it has been waiting for me.”

“For what?”

“To finish.”

They climbed the stairs.

In every gallery, objects were disappearing. Not destroyed, but released. The model ship grew sails and vanished into a painted sea. The abandoned chess player moved her queen. Blank faces appeared in portraits, smiling uncertainly.

At the entrance, the brass sign fell from above the doors.

Mr. Vale picked it up.

**NOT YET COMPLETE**, it still read.

He turned it over.

On the other side were two different words:

**BEGIN AGAIN**

He gave the sign to Mara.

“Can a museum do that?” she asked.

“A museum can do anything once no one is curating it.”

Outside, the rain had stopped. Dawn touched the rooftops.

Mara’s mother stood beneath a streetlamp, still wearing her nightdress under a hastily buttoned coat. Her hair was wet, her face pale with fear.

“Mara!”

This time, Mara knew the voice.

She ran down the steps.

Her mother caught her so tightly it hurt. She demanded to know where Mara had been, why her bed was empty, why she had taken the jar, what she had been thinking.

Mara answered none of the questions.

She only listened.

Her mother’s voice was lower than she had remembered. It cracked when she was frightened. Certain words carried the faint accent of a town she had left as a child.

It was not the voice Mara had tried to preserve.

It was better.

Over her mother’s shoulder, Mara looked back.

Mr. Vale stood in the museum doorway, his silver hair bright in the rising sun.

“What will you do now?” she called.

He considered the question.

“I was once a clockmaker.”

“Do you remember how?”

“No.”

Mara smiled. “Then you can learn.”

Mr. Vale smiled too.

He closed the museum doors.

By the time Mara and her mother reached the corner, the building was gone. Between the abandoned bakery and the windowless house stood an empty lot filled with tall grass.

Years later, Mara sometimes wondered whether the museum had existed at all.

She remembered enough to believe it had.

She also remembered enough to doubt.

She grew older. She finished school, though not every assignment. She studied marine biology, abandoned it, and became a carpenter instead. She built tables, cabinets, boats, and once a spiral staircase for a house overlooking the sea.

She made mistakes. She left projects incomplete. She forgot birthdays and lost photographs. She argued with her mother and sometimes apologized too late.

But every July, Mara swam to the black rock.

The first time, she went alone.

The water was colder than it had been in the jar. The distance was greater. Halfway there, she nearly turned back.

When she finally climbed onto the rock, she found it rough, gray, and covered with sharp barnacles. It was nothing like the smooth black island from her memory.

Mara sat there until sunset.

She did not see Eli.

She did not hear him call.

But when the wind crossed the water, she remembered something he had once said—not on the beach, but in the hospital, near the end.

She had forgotten the words for years.

“You don’t have to finish for both of us,” he had whispered. “Just keep going.”

Mara looked toward the shore, where lights had begun to shine in the windows of the town.

Then she slipped back into the sea and swam home.
